title: Shuttle Smart-bombing Is Anti-Gameplay, Not PvP

posts.name: Calder Briggs
posts.cooked:
Smart-bombing shuttles at gates is one of the most harmful and least defensible mechanics still present in EVE Online. It is not meaningful PvP, it is not emergent gameplay, and it is not harsh-but-fair. It is a non-interactive, low-effort, high-frustration mechanic that punishes the wrong players and adds nothing of value to the game.

The Mechanic Is Completely Non-Interactive
Smart-bombing shuttles removes all player agency.
The victim cannot react or cannot counter,
The attacker requires no timing, no piloting, no decision-making, no risk, and no skill expression.
This is not PvP. It is a predetermined execution that violates EVE’s core design philosophy of meaningful player choice.

the so-called “counterplay” of warping to another celestial first is not a real solution. It does not teach anything meaningful. It does not reward awareness, skill, or decision-making. It simply forces players to add even more tedious travel time to an already massive universe.

Expecting players to make two or three extra warps per system just to maybe avoid a handful of people abusing a zero-interaction mechanic is not gameplay. It is not risk management. It is not clever piloting. It is just wasting the player’s time. A mechanic that requires players to triple their travel actions just to maybe avoid dying to something they cannot see, cannot react to, and cannot counter is not a mechanic worth defending.

It Creates Rage-Inducing Loss With No Lesson Learned
EVE’s harshness works when the player learns something from a loss. Smart-bombing shuttles teach nothing. There is no lesson except “do not undock in a shuttle” and “You must add an excessive amount of travel time”. Loss without learning is bad game design and directly harms player retention.

It Turns Travel Into Punishment, Not Gameplay
Travel in EVE is already slow and tedious.
Smart-bombing shuttles turn it into a punishment loop:
Lose shuttle, rebuy, re-travel, re-attempt the same route. “no one wants to take 30minutes to scout for the right wormhole connection”.

A single death can add 30 to 90 minutes of wasted time.
This is not risk versus reward. It is risk versus frustration.

It Actively Drives Players Away From the Game
Smart-bombing shuttles are one of the most common “Alt-F4 and never come back” moments for new and returning players.
CCP’s own retention data has shown that:
Unfair, non-interactive deaths are the most damaging to new player retention.
Travel-related deaths are among the highest churn events.
Losses that feel cheap or rigged cause players to quit.
This mechanic directly contributes to player churn.

It Adds No Meaningful Content to the Game
Smart-bombing shuttles provide:
No strategic value
No escalation
No counter-escalation
No “meaningful” killmails
No conflict drivers
No story
No content
Even the players who do it admit they do it for the salt, not for gameplay.

This mechanic rewards the worst kind of people and behavior:
Low effort, low risk, high annoyance, zero creativity.
It is griefing disguised as PvP.

Rebuttal: The Argument “Just Don’t Warp Gate-to-Gate”
This is the most common defense of smart-bombing, and it is also the weakest.

A. It Shifts Responsibility Away From Bad Mechanics
Telling players to warp to a celestial first is not a solution.
It is blaming the victim for a mechanic that has no real counterplay.

B. It Adds Tedium, Not Gameplay
Warping to a celestial adds 10 to 20 seconds per jump, 5 to 10 minutes per route, and 30 to 60 minutes per long trip.
It adds nothing fun, interesting, or skillful.
It is a time tax, not counterplay.

C. It Punishes Newer Players the Most
Established veterans with lots of money, scouts, alts, jump-bridges do not care.
New and solo players do.
Telling them to add 30 minutes of detours is dismissive and unhelpful.

D. It Is Not Reliable
Smartbombers can reposition, use multiple alts, sit on celestials, or simply catch you on the next gate anyway.
It is a coin flip with extra steps.

E. It Contradicts EVE’s Own Design Philosophy
Real gatecamps can be scouted, avoided, countered, or fought.
Smartbombing shuttles cannot.
Warping to a celestial does not change that.

F. It Is a Lazy Defense of a reprehensible Mechanic
If the only counterplay to a mechanic is adding 30 minutes of pointless travel time, then the mechanic is the problem, not the player.

Conclusion
Smartbombing shuttles at gates should be removed or fixed because it is non-interactive, unskilled, unfun, disproportionately harmful, rage-inducing, retention-killing, contentless, and fundamentally bad design.

EVE can remain dangerous, unpredictable, and punishing without relying on cheap, low-effort mechanics that punish the wrong players and add nothing to the game.

This is not about making EVE fair.
It is about rewarding interaction, decision-making, and gameplay that actually engages players instead of driving them away.

posts.name: Calder Briggs
posts.cooked:
Sounds like a lazy response to me.

“Farming salt IS core EVE gameplay.”

Farming salt is a side effect of EVE’s gameplay — not the gameplay itself.
Salt comes from interaction, conflict, risk, loss, outplay, mistakes, and player decisions.

Smartbombing shuttles has none of that.

There is:

  • no interaction

  • no decision-making

  • no piloting

  • no scouting

  • no counterplay

  • no risk

  • no escalation

  • no story

If your “salt farming” requires the target to be literally incapable of interacting with you, then it’s not EVE gameplay — it’s a loading‑screen execution.

Salt is supposed to be the byproduct of conflict, not the only reason the mechanic exists.

posts.name: Dominai
posts.cooked:
Shuttles already have near-instant warp. In high-sec, catching them through normal locking is already almost impossible. If smartbombing shuttles is removed globally, especially in high-sec, shuttle travel becomes almost completely risk-free.

posts.name: Calder Briggs
posts.cooked:
“Shuttles already have near‑instant warp… removing smartbombing makes travel risk‑free.”

Shuttles are not supposed to be “dangerous ships.” They are travel tools, the same way pods are. The danger in EVE is supposed to come from interaction, not from unavoidable, zero‑agency executions.

Real risk in EVE comes from:
instalockers
drag bubbles
gatecamps
hunters
combat probes
actual PvP

All of those involve interaction, decision‑making, piloting, scouting, and counterplay.

Smart-bombing shuttles involves none of that. It’s a loading‑screen kill.

Removing a zero‑interaction mechanic does not make travel risk‑free. It makes travel “gameplay‑based”, instead of “RNG +Time-dump based”.

And if the complaint is that people can move things in shuttles, or that pods and shuttles are nearly impossible to catch through normal means, then CCP can design around that. That’s literally their job.

If the problem is “shuttles are too safe,” CCP can:
create a no‑cargo micro‑shuttle
create a travel‑only hull with zero storage
adjust warp speeds
adjust align times
adjust sig radius
adjust HP
add new travel mechanics

There are dozens of ways to address the concern without relying on a mechanic that kills players before they can even load grid.

And honestly—what’s the harm in people being able to move around the extremely vast game they’ve created?

posts.name: Dominai
posts.cooked:
Making shuttles realistically lockable defeats the purpose of shuttles as fast travel ships. But exempting them from smartbombs would make them effectively risk-free in high-sec and low-sec. That is why I do not think removing smartbomb interaction is the right fix.

If a player wants safer travel against smartbombs, there are already options for that, such as travel-fit interceptors or other more survivable travel ships. Those choices come with tradeoffs, which is exactly how EVE balance should work.

Making any ship effectively immune to a specific weapon mechanic is a terrible precedent.

posts.name: Calder Briggs
posts.cooked:
I get where you’re coming from — shuttles do warp quickly, and yes, CCP has to be careful not to make travel completely trivial. But removing smartbombing from shuttles doesn’t make them “risk‑free,” it just removes the only threat in the game that kills them before the player can even load grid.

Shuttles are already vulnerable to plenty of interactive dangers:
instalockers
drag bubbles
gatecamps
hunters
combat probes
pipe camps
wormhole rollers
station/undock smartbombs
smartbombs on anything other than gates

I have been murdered in shuttles by all of these.

All of these involve scouting, piloting, decision‑making, or counterplay. Smartbombing shuttles is the only one that bypasses all of that and kills the player before they can even see what happened.

And suggesting a travel‑fit interceptor as the “safer option” doesn’t really address the issue '“especially for new or solo players”. A T2 ship with rigs, modules, Omega skills, and a price tag is not a substitute for a basic, disposable, non‑aggressive travel tool. Shuttles should exist so players can move themselves — not cargo, not value — just themselves. Not everyone moving between staging systems, joining fleets, or returning to the game should be forced into a T2 hull just to avoid a zero‑interaction death, or be forced to add additional time to maneuver between 3-4 celestial objects for each and every system in a 10+ route.

If the concern is that shuttles can move items or are too hard to catch, CCP can solve that directly without relying on a mechanic that deletes players before they load grid. They can create no‑cargo micro‑shuttles, adjust HP or sig, or add new travel hulls. There are plenty of design levers that preserve interactive danger without adding even more time tax to a game where travel is already one of the most time‑consuming activities.

The goal isn’t to make travel safe — it’s to make danger interactive. Smartbombing shuttles is the opposite of that.

posts.name: Gerard Amatin
posts.cooked:
Calder Briggs:

The Mechanic Is Completely Non-Interactive
Smart-bombing shuttles removes all player agency.

Incorrect.

As competent player have complete control over between which two locations you wish your shuttle to warp.
As competent player you have the tools to check for any risk of smartbombing ships in system and on the path you wish to warp.

In other words, you have a lot of player agency in the choices you made right before you died.

Smartbombs have a surprisingly short range. If a smartbomber is set up on the shuttle path between objects A and B, it is as simple as ‘bouncing’ of object C on your route to B to completely avoid the smartbomb range.

Have I died to smartbombs mid-warp?

Sure.

Totally my bad too, I could easily have avoided that but was lazy and inattentive. Lost a bunch of implants to people who we were at war with, so it was fair game too.

Smartbombing shuttles is an essential part of EVE. Unlike most other ships, shuttles are nigh-impossible to catch the conventional way with weapons which rely on targeting due to their sub 2 second align time.

Shuttles however need also to be part of the interaction in EVE and we should be able to kill shuttles.

After all, shuttles can be used by scouts to fly ahead of fleets and keep track of hostiles. Shuttles can be used by scammers to post their spam contracts in local chat. Shuttles can be used to carry billions and billions of blueprints:

zkillboard.com

Caldari Shuttle | hogfatt | Killmail

hogfatt (Fatt Hogs Corp) lost their Caldari Shuttle in Kinakka (Black Rise). Final Blow by Rakaz (Know-Nothings) flying in a Machariel. Total Value: 19,974,653,250.93 ISK

And like any other ship with strategic value like that, we should be able to interact with it and kill it. But how can someone kill an cheap interdiction nullified ship when it almost cannot be targeted?

Smartbombs.

Just don’t blindly warp gate-to-gate and your shuttle will be fine. There is your player agency.

posts.name: Calder Briggs
posts.cooked:
Gerard, To “properly” scout for smartbombers on a route, you need another pilot going ahead of you. That means a second account, multiboxing, and treating basic shuttle travel like a coordinated op. So when you say “competent players can check for risk,” what you’re really saying is: every player should have multiple accounts and run a scout for a non‑combat shuttle with no cargo.

That’s not reasonable, especially for new or returning players, or anyone who just wants to move themselves between systems.

And even with a scout, smartbombers are often not visible until it’s too late. They can sit off‑grid, on mid‑warp bookmarks, cloaked, logged off, or simply be on a different gate than the one your scout just checked. By the time your shuttle is in warp, the decision is already locked in. If the camp is there, you die before you even see the grid. That’s not meaningful agency, that’s a coin flip. and taking 2-5 minutes to verify each and every single ship and player in the system is unreasonable.

Travel in EVE is already one of the most time‑consuming parts of the game. Your answer to that is: add more time, add more accounts, add more paranoia. Bounce every gate, scout every system, treat every undock like a covert ops mission. That isn’t good gameplay, it’s a time and account tax.

Shuttles are non‑combat travel tools. They’re already vulnerable to interactive danger previously mentioned. They are not “risk‑free.” The only thing they’re mostly immune to is targeted locking, which is intentional because they’re not combat ships.

Smartbombing shuttles is the outlier because it bypasses all interaction. It kills before grid loads, before the player can react, and often in ways that no reasonable, realistic amount of scouting or caution will prevent unless you’re multiboxing and traveling like a paranoid veteran.

There are plenty of ways to keep shuttles part of the ecosystem without relying on a zero‑interaction mechanic that mostly just punishes people for trying to move around.

The issue isn’t “shuttles must never die.” The issue is that they shouldn’t die to a bull**** gotcha mechanic. Even adding a little more health to shuttles or how the damage applies so players don’t insta-die before grid loads, could solve the problem.

posts.name: Slop4Slop
posts.cooked:
The Anti-Smartbomb Argument Is Really Just an Elaborate Temper Tantrum

What makes these recurring anti-smartbomb essays so fascinating is not the argument itself—because the argument is rarely new—but the underlying assumption that keeps slipping through the cracks.

The author clearly believes that every death in EVE should arrive with advance notice, visible warning signs, ample reaction time, multiple layers of counterplay, and a clear educational lesson tailored specifically to the victim’s personal growth journey.

In other words, they want a game that constantly protects them from the consequences of their own decisions.

And that has never been EVE.

The entire essay is built on the premise that smartbombing is illegitimate because the victim cannot react after initiating warp.

But this is only persuasive if you pretend the player materialized in warp against their will.

Nobody forced them onto that route.

Nobody forced them into that ship.

Nobody forced them to use the fastest possible travel method.

Nobody forced them to ignore known risks.

The argument repeatedly removes every decision the traveler made and then concludes there was no player agency.

That is like sprinting across a highway without looking both ways and then declaring automobiles an unfair game mechanic.

The “There Is No Counterplay” Complaint

This is where the argument stops being serious and starts sounding like a child arguing that chores are impossible because they require standing up.

The counterplay exists.

Everyone knows it exists.

Even the author spends several paragraphs explaining the counterplay.

Then immediately argues that it doesn’t count because it takes time.

Think about how absurd that position actually is.

The complaint is not:

“The counterplay doesn’t work.”

The complaint is:

“The counterplay is annoying.”

Those are completely different arguments.

By that standard, nearly every defensive measure in EVE could be dismissed.

Scouting takes time.

Intel channels take time.

Creating bookmarks takes time.

Moving fleets takes time.

Checking maps takes time.

Watching local takes attention.

Managing risk requires effort.

Welcome to EVE.

The author treats every additional warp as though CCP is demanding players carry bricks uphill.

In reality we’re talking about clicking a celestial before warping.

The level of outrage is wildly disproportionate to the inconvenience being described.

The “No Lesson Learned” Argument Is Especially Funny

Apparently every loss in EVE is now required to provide a personalized educational experience.

This is a fascinating standard.

Imagine applying it elsewhere.

A player gets baited into a cyno trap.

“No lesson learned.”

A player gets scammed.

“No lesson learned.”

A player jumps into a bubble.

“No lesson learned.”

A player undocks a freighter through Uedama and explodes.

“No lesson learned.”

Of course lessons exist.

The author simply doesn’t like them.

The lesson is:

“Traveling through dangerous space carries risk.”

The lesson is:

“Fastest is not always safest.”

The lesson is:

“Knowledge matters.”

The lesson is:

“Preparation matters.”

The lesson is:

“Assuming nothing bad will happen is not a strategy.”

These are lessons EVE has been teaching for over twenty years.

The real complaint seems to be that the lesson was delivered in a way the victim found emotionally upsetting.

The Retention Argument Is Mostly Emotional Blackmail

Like many weak arguments, this one eventually reaches for the nuclear option:

“Think of the new players.”

We’re told that smartbombing causes people to quit.

We’re told it damages retention.

We’re told it drives players away.

Curiously, concrete evidence is never provided.

Instead we’re expected to assume that any mechanic generating frustration must therefore be bad for the game.

But EVE’s entire identity is built around losses that are memorable precisely because they hurt.

The game has survived for decades despite scams, betrayals, gate camps, piracy, ganking, theft, espionage, market manipulation, and every other unpleasant surprise players have invented.

Yet somehow the true existential threat to the game is a shuttle exploding on a gate.

At some point this stops sounding like concern for retention and starts sounding like someone trying to elevate a personal annoyance into a design crisis.

The Most Revealing Part

The most revealing thing about the entire essay is the language.

Everything is described in terms of frustration.

Everything is described in terms of annoyance.

Everything is described in terms of inconvenience.

Very little is described in terms of mechanics.

That’s because this is not fundamentally a mechanical argument.

It’s an emotional one.

The author encountered a consequence they disliked.

The consequence felt unfair.

Therefore the mechanic must be unfair.

The consequence felt frustrating.

Therefore the mechanic must be bad.

The consequence interrupted their plans.

Therefore the mechanic must be removed.

This is not game design analysis.

This is the rhetorical equivalent of a toddler throwing a toy across the room because it didn’t behave the way they wanted.

Conclusion

Smartbombing is not beloved because it is noble.

It is not beloved because it is honorable.

It is not beloved because it produces cinematic duels.

It is tolerated because it occupies a small, predictable, avoidable niche within a game built around risk and player knowledge.

The strongest criticism presented against it is not that it lacks counterplay.

It is not that it lacks counters.

It is not that it lacks warning signs.

It is that avoiding it requires effort.

And once you strip away the dramatic language, the retention panic, the appeals to fairness, and the lengthy descriptions of how upsetting the experience feels, the entire argument boils down to a remarkably simple complaint:

“I don’t want to take precautions, and I don’t think I should have to.”

Unfortunately for the author, EVE Online has spent more than twenty years teaching players that dangerous space does not care what they think they should have to do.

posts.name: Calder Briggs
posts.cooked:
Dyver, you’re throwing around words like “counterplay,” “decision‑making,” and “story” as if repeating them makes them true. So let’s be specific: what counterplay are you actually talking about? Because the only “decision‑making” involved in smartbombing shuttles is choosing whichever gate has the most traffic and pressing F1 on a multibox setup.

That’s not interaction. That’s not piloting. That’s not PvP. That’s farming.

And no, scouting isn’t the magical solution you’re pretending it is. To scout a route properly, you need another pilot physically entering each system ahead of you. That means a second account, multiboxing, and treating basic shuttle travel like a covert‑ops infiltration. If your argument is “just assume every gate is smartbombed and play accordingly,” then you’re admitting the mechanic forces players into permanent paranoia just to move around.

That’s not counterplay. That’s a time tax and an account tax.

Your “contacts list” argument doesn’t hold up either. There is no universal list of smartbombers. Every region has different groups, different alts, different corps, different time zones, different cloaky setups. Compiling a meaningful list would take weeks, and even then it wouldn’t solve or mend the problem. You’re describing a fantasy version of intel that doesn’t exist for new players or even some Vets, then theres returning players, or anyone who isn’t already deeply embedded in lowsec politics or knows the depth sectors of space like the chud who lives inside this game.

And others calling this “essential gameplay” is wild. Every 1v1, every fleet fight, every wormhole brawl, every roam, every hunt — those all tell stories. Entire YouTube channels exist because real PvP has narrative, escalation, choices, mistakes, triumphs, and losses. Smartbombing shuttles has none of that. It’s the opposite of story. It’s a loading‑screen execution.

If the peak of gameplay for you is sitting on a gate with a multibox smartbomb fleet deleting shuttles and pods before the pilot even loads grid, then just say that. But don’t pretend it’s deep, interactive, or meaningful. It’s not. It’s a zero‑interaction trap that punishes nearly everyone, wastes our valuable time, and adds nothing to the game except frustration.

If EVE genuinely expects players to treat every undock like a covert ops mission, assume every gate is a trap, maintain a personal database of smartbombers, and multibox scouts just to move themselves between systems, then CCP should put that in the marketing: “EVE Online — the most complicated, obscure, and unforgiving travel simulator ever made.”

Because that’s what you’re defending.

posts.name: Calder Briggs
posts.cooked:
Gerard, I do appreciate the way you’re engaging with the structure of what I’m saying. But I think we need to be honest about the practical side of the advice you’re giving.

Why would anyone want to run a 5‑degree d‑scan at every gate? Even doing it more than once or twice per trip is already too much, “obviously not the case with other ships though.”.

Turning basic travel into a sequence of constant scans, bounces, and checks isn’t engaging gameplay—it’s just tedious. When someone is simply trying to move from A to B in a pod or a shuttle, they shouldn’t have to treat every system like a covert‑ops operation. “unless their fleeing in their implant pod from just getting popped”
[WHY ARE YOU RUNNIN!!] -meme

And this isn’t happening in a vacuum. EVE already leans heavily in favor of veteran players who know every trick, every trap, every name, every region. New players and returning players don’t have that background. They don’t have a mental map of who smartbombs where. They don’t have a curated contact list. They don’t have the experience to know that “you should always assume every gate is a smartbomb trap” is even a thing. And you shouldn’t have to if you’re purely traveling.

I’ve seen some of the shuttle kills you’re talking about. I’ve seen people lose researched BPOs because they thought a shuttle was the safe option—and then they never logged in again. That’s not a rare story. It’s not hypothetical. It’s something people can verify on zKillboard: when the killmail is the last activity on the character.

So I’m genuinely curious how you would describe multibox smartbombing shuttles as meaningful or healthy for the game. What does it add? How does it improve the experience for anyone except the person running the multibox setup? Because from the perspective of someone just trying to travel, it feels less like “emergent gameplay” and more like a punishment for not treating every single undock as a high‑stakes infiltration mission.

That’s the core of my point: the amount of effort required to avoid this one specific mechanic is wildly out of proportion to the value it brings to the game.

P.S. I like how your comments are structured. How are you inputting my quotes in there like that?

I have to say I am a bit split on the issue.

On one hand I can see how it is kinda “fun” for those farming salt and/or getting kinda “jackpot” every like thousand (?) shuttle bombings because some idiot really had a BPO or something inside…

On the other hand I see the frustration of many who just wanted to reach an OP system or get back home because they died in the last OP and either you take 3 times as long for your route by having bouncespots and dscan check gates (which isn’t possible everywhere because of distances and sometimes not even a warpable celestial is near to the stargate you need to take, so you either warp to 50km, then rewarp, then again warp to the gate if it is clear…). Or you cross fingers and then suddenly “beep beep, wake up in Jita again”.
It’s not about the loss, even if the pod is empty it’s just wasted time to do those 20, 30, 40 jumps again and maybe even miss a fleet you’d wanted to go to. I have indeed seen players logging off and not playing that day any more because it just killed the fun for them.

So my usual approach is: What would benefit the game itself (as a product on a competitive market) more?
I usually don’t die to Smartbombs because I literally have bounce spots in almost every lowsec system, but in the greater picture I feel that mechanic is more an annoyance than a benefit for the majority of the players.
I am absolutely not a player that wants to make “everything totally safe”, but at least attach some skill to killing mechanics. And to be honest, Shuttle smartbombing is a 100% no skill activity. I have done it, either the guy warps via a bounce spot then you won’t get him, or he doesn’t and you get him 100% of the time if he lands in your SB range. In my opinion Smartbombs should just fire at the end of their cycle instead of instant, so they still work as firewalls or drone deterrent in combat, but if you want to catch shuttles or pods, you’d need to run them constantly with each one having a delay to the other and not just 1-click-kill things firing them all. I’d have no problem with removing Shuttle cargo in return, I don’t think the game needs the capability to transport items in shuttles, if someone wants to transport stuff, either a speedy frig or a blockaderunner will do perfectly fine.
I know that opinion might not be popular among the “EVE is so crazy hardcore crowd” but nonetheless, from my PoV the game would be a better one with smartbombing actually requiring some skill, at least more than it takes now.
